subject: physics
title: Charged particles in magnetic fields
key_idea: A charged particle moving across a magnetic field feels a force F = BQv sin θ at right angles to its velocity. The force does no work, so a particle moving at right angles to the field travels in a circle of radius mv/(BQ).

blocks.text: A moving charge is a tiny current, so a magnetic field exerts a force on it. The force depends on the charge, its speed and the field.

blocks.label: Force on a moving charge
where: θ = angle between the velocity and the field

items: When the velocity is at right angles to the field, F = BQv.
When the velocity is along the field, the force is zero.
The force is at right angles to both the velocity and the field.

items.text: For a wire, F = BIL.
A charge Q takes time t = L/v to travel a length L, so the current is I = Q/t = Qv/L.
F = B × (Qv/L) × L = BQv.

items: Use Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger along the field, thumb gives the force.
The second finger points along the conventional current, which is the direction a positive charge moves.
For a negative charge such as an electron, the current is opposite to the velocity. The force is therefore in the opposite direction to that on a positive charge moving the same way.
F = BQv sin θ.
The force is perpendicular to the velocity, and reverses for a charge of opposite sign.

sections.heading: Circular motion in a magnetic field

blocks.text: A force always at right angles to the velocity changes the direction of motion but not the speed. The particle moves in a circle.

items: The magnetic force does no work on the particle, because it is always at right angles to the motion.
The kinetic energy and speed stay constant.
The circle lies in a plane at right angles to the field.

items.text: The force on the particle is BQv.
Circular motion needs a centripetal force mv²/r, and the magnetic force provides it.
BQv = mv²/r, so r = mv/(BQ).

items: The time for one circuit is T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(BQ). It does not depend on the speed.
A faster particle moves in a larger circle but takes the same time.
A stronger field gives a smaller circle. A heavier particle gives a larger circle.
If the velocity is not at right angles to the field, only the component at right angles circles. The path becomes a helix.

diagram.alt: A slider activity. Choose a particle, its speed and the magnetic flux density and see the radius of its circular path and the time for one circuit.

items: A magnetic force on a moving charge acts as the centripetal force.
r = mv/(BQ), and the time for one circuit is independent of speed.

blocks.text: Electric and magnetic fields at right angles can select particles of one speed from a beam. The forces on a particle act in opposite directions.

items.text: The electric field E exerts a force QE on the particle, in one direction.
The magnetic field B exerts a force BQv on the particle in the opposite direction.
A particle with QE = BQv feels no resultant force and passes straight through.

blocks.label: Speed of the particles that pass straight through

items: The charge cancels, so the selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass.
Slower particles feel a larger electric force than magnetic force and are deflected one way. Faster particles are deflected the other way.
A narrow slit at the exit lets only the undeflected particles through.
Particles pass undeflected when electric and magnetic forces are equal.
The selected speed is v = E/B.

checks.q: An electron travels at 2.0 × 10⁷ m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 mT. Calculate the radius of its path. (Electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
Explain why a magnetic field does not change the speed of a charged particle moving in it.
checks.a: The force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work on the particle. Its kinetic energy and speed are constant and only its direction changes.

checks.q: Charged particles pass undeflected through crossed electric and magnetic fields. E = 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.040 T. Calculate their speed.

blocks.text: A cyclotron accelerates charged particles to high energies in a vacuum. It uses the fact that the time for a half-turn does not depend on speed.

items.text: Two hollow D-shaped electrodes are placed in a uniform magnetic field at right angles to them.
A particle crossing the gap between the dees is accelerated by an alternating p.d.
Inside a dee there is no electric field. The magnetic field makes the particle move in a semicircle.
The half-turn takes πm/(BQ), which is the same at every speed. The p.d. alternates at the constant frequency f = BQ/(2πm).
Each crossing adds energy. The speed grows, so the radius grows and the path spirals outwards to the edge.

items: The alternating p.d. has a fixed frequency because the half-turn time is constant.
The path is a spiral of increasing radius.

blocks.text: When a current flows along a thin slice of conductor in a magnetic field at right angles to the slice, a small p.d. appears across its width.

items.text: The magnetic force pushes the moving charge carriers towards one edge of the slice.
Charge builds up on that edge and an electric field develops across the slice.
The sideways electric force on a carrier grows until it equals the magnetic force. Then the carriers go straight again.
The p.d. across the slice at this stage is the Hall voltage Vₕ.
qVₕ / d = Bqv, where d is the width of the slice. So Vₕ = Bvd.
I = nAvq with A = dt, so v = I / (ndtq).
Vₕ = B × I / (ndtq) × d = BI / (ntq).

blocks.label: Hall voltage
where: n = number density of charge carriers (m⁻³)

items: A Hall probe is a thin slice of semiconductor carrying a constant current.
For a constant current, Vₕ is proportional to B, so the probe is calibrated to read B.
A semiconductor has a small n, which gives a large Vₕ.
The flat face of the slice must be at right angles to the field.
Vₕ = BI/(ntq).
A Hall probe measures flux density from the Hall voltage.
